Every number printed there matches a step of the hand arithmetic: 39.2, then 1536.64, then
384.16, then 385.

Try it 12.5: price up a tighter benchmark

Your department wants a benchmark that pins a model’s accuracy to within 3 percentage points
either way, at 95 percent confidence.

How many questions does that take? Show all six steps.

Compare it with the 385 questions needed for 5 percentage points. Is the extra cost
proportional to the extra precision?

Solution

1. Use Formula 12.9 with h = 0.03 and the worst case \hat{p} = 0.5.

Step 1, write down what you want. h = 0.03, \hat{p} = 0.5.

Step 2, divide. 1.96 \div 0.03 = 65.333333

Step 3, square. 65.333333 \times 65.333333 = 4268.444

Step 4, the share product. 0.5 \times 0.5 = 0.25

Step 5, multiply. 4268.444 \times 0.25 = 1067.111

Step 6, round up. \mathbf{1068} questions.

2. No, and the mismatch is the lesson. Going from a half-width of 5 points to a half-width
of 3 points improves the precision by a factor of 5 \div 3 = 1.6667. The cost goes from 385
questions to 1,068 questions, which is a factor of 1068 \div 385 = 2.7740.

Check that against the square: 1.6667 \times 1.6667 = 2.7779. That is not quite the 2.7740
above, and the gap is step 6, where both answers were rounded up to a whole question. Before
that rounding the cost went from 384.16 questions to 1067.111 questions, and
1067.111 \div 384.16 = 2.7778. The cost grows with the square of the precision gain, which
is the square root in Formula 12.2 read backwards.

Notice also where 1,068 sits. Miller’s recommendation of at least 1,000 questions is very close
to the number you need for a plus or minus 3 point interval in the worst case. That
recommendation is not a round number somebody liked. It is this arithmetic.

hierarchy.lvl2: Common mistakes
Common mistakes

records.content:
Numbered, so you can be told “that is number 4” and know what is meant.

Reporting a score without an interval. “The model scored 25 percent” is not a result. “25
percent, 95 percent interval 6 percent to 44 percent, on 20 questions” is a result. If you
report the first one, the reader cannot tell whether your model beats guessing.

Thinking the wobble comes from the model. The model in this chapter is deterministic. Run
it a thousand times on these twenty questions and it gives the same five right answers every
time. The variability is in which questions got asked, not in the model. People look for
the randomness in the wrong place and then conclude, wrongly, that fixing the seed or setting
temperature to zero removes the need for an interval.

Trusting the Wald interval near 0 or 1. At 8 right out of 10 it returns an upper end of
104.79 percent. Before using it, check that there are a decent number of right answers and
a decent number of wrong answers. Ten of each is the usual rule of thumb. When that fails,
use Wilson.

Chopping an impossible interval off at 1. Turning (0.5521, 1.0479) into
(0.5521, 1.0000) looks like a fix and is not one. Wilson gives (0.4902, 0.9433), which is
lower at both ends. Trimming the top leaves the bottom wrong.

Confusing percent with percentage points. Moving from 20 percent to 30 percent is a rise
of 10 percentage points and also a rise of 50 percent. The standard error of 0.0968 is 9.68
percentage points. Saying “9.68 percent” means something different and usually something
false. See 

Toolkit 11.

Believing more resamples means more certainty. Going from 10,000 resamples to 1,000,000
does not narrow your interval, because it does not add a single question. More resamples only
smooth out the simulation’s own noise. The bootstrap cannot overcome a small sample; it can
only show you how small it is.

Reporting more digits than the test can produce. A twenty-question test produces scores in
steps of 5 percentage points. Writing 25.0 percent is fine; writing 25.03 percent is not,
because that number cannot occur. Check that the score you print is one the test can
actually give.

Rounding partway through and then reporting extra digits. Round once, at the end. Rounding
the standard error to 0.0968 and then reporting the interval to five decimal places claims a
precision you threw away two steps earlier.

Averaging two disagreeing runs and reporting the average. If two runs of the same
benchmark differ, that difference is a measurement about your pipeline. Report both, then
explain. The average hides the finding.

Reading a confidence interval as a probability about the truth. The careful statement is
about the procedure: a method that, used repeatedly, captures the true value about 95
times in 100. In practice the useful reading is “values in this range are consistent with
what I saw, and values outside it are not”, and that reading will not get you into trouble.

hierarchy.lvl2: What to remember
What to remember

records.content:
A benchmark score is a sample proportion, so it is a quantity that moves when the questions
change, not a fixed property of the model. The size of that movement is the standard error,
\sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})/n}, which was 0.0968 on our twenty-question run and turns into a Wald
interval from 6.0 percent to 44.0 percent, or 11.19 percent to 46.87 percent once the Wilson
formula repairs it for a count that small. The textbook Wald formula carries assumptions and
breaks near 0 and 1, returning an accuracy of 104.79 percent at 8 right out of 10, where Wilson
correctly returns 0.4902 to 0.9433. The bootstrap reaches nearly the same answer by resampling
instead of by formula, 5.0 percent to 45.0 percent, and it also reveals that a twenty-question
test can only produce scores 5 percentage points apart and disagreed with itself on 79.9 percent
of resamples. Report the interval, report the number of questions, and if you want a score good
to within 3 percentage points, ask 1,068 questions.

intervals overlap, and concludes that the models are indistinguishable. Explain why comparing
two separate intervals is the wrong analysis for this design, and describe in words what a
better analysis would use instead. 

Chapter 13 does this properly; answer from the
idea, not from the formula.

Where this goes next

This chapter put an interval around a number and found the number could not carry the weight
that was put on it. 

Chapter 13 asks a harder question: whether the number was
measuring what you thought at all.

The model in this chapter scored exactly 25.0 percent on a four-option test, which is exactly
what blind guessing scores. That is a coincidence worth investigating, and it does not survive
investigation.

records.content:
It is a Tuesday in July. You step outside in Bakersfield and the air has that flat, heavy
quality you know. You pull out your phone and look up the air quality for the day.

You get a number.

Now ask a harder question. What is that number a number of? Before anyone can answer, they
have to tell you four other things. Which pollutant is being reported, because particle
pollution and ozone are different substances measured by different instruments. Over what
window, because the rule for ozone reads an eight-hour stretch and the rule for fine particles
reads a full day. Measured where, because a monitor beside a freeway and a monitor in a field
outside Shafter are breathing different air. And reported how, because a scale that combines
several pollutants into one headline figure has to decide what to do when they disagree.

Change any one of those four decisions and the headline number changes. Nobody lied. Every
version was computed correctly. The air did not change between one version and the next. What
changed was the procedure, and the number belongs to the procedure at least as much as it
belongs to the air.

This is not a complaint about air monitoring. Air monitoring is a serious, careful field, and
the reason it publishes its rules in public documents that run to hundreds of pages is precisely
that everybody in it understands the point you are about to learn. The rules are written down so
that the number means something.

Now hold that thought and look at how artificial intelligence gets reported. A model scores
some per cent on some benchmark. The score appears in a press release, on a leaderboard, in a
purchasing decision, in a news story. The rule that produced it is usually one line in an
appendix, if it appears at all.

This chapter takes one small model, one set of twenty questions, and three different rules for
marking the answers. All three rules are defensible. All three appear in published research.
Nothing about the model changes between them. Nothing about the questions changes.

The three numbers are 25.0%, 35.0% and 15.0%.

You are going to compute all three, work out which of them, if any, deserves to be printed, and
then find out something worse: that the answer is none of them.

Where the numbers in this chapter came from

Every measured number in this chapter was produced by a script in the course repository and
written to a file you can open.

The three scoring procedures: lab/we6b_eval_debiased.py wrote lab/out/we6b_eval_debiased.json.

The three model sizes: lab/lab4_size_ladder.py wrote lab/out/lab4_size_ladder.json.

The two-model comparison: lab/we7_paired_comparison.py wrote lab/out/we7_paired.json.

The question bank is twenty multiple-choice questions about general-education statistics,
four options each, exactly one correct. They were written by hand for this course by your
instructor. They are not a published benchmark, nobody else uses them, and they have no standing
outside this book. All twenty are listed in


the datasets appendix, section 3.2, with each question’s topic and its
correct letter, and the four options of every question are printed in the lab script that used
them, lab/we6b_eval_debiased.py. Saying that plainly matters, because the whole argument of
this chapter is about how little twenty questions can settle, and that argument only works if you
know exactly what you are holding.

The rule of this book is we never publish a number we did not compute. One worked example in
this chapter, in Formula 13.5, uses invented log-probabilities, because small numbers are easier
to check by hand, and it is labelled made up for practice where it appears. Try it 13.3, Try
it 13.4 and Try it 13.5 invent their tables and their scenarios, and each says so at the top of
the box. The practice problems invent theirs too, and the line above the first problem says so.
Every other number on this page is a measurement, and the file it came out of is named beside it.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

Explain why an evaluation score is a property of the scoring procedure as much as of the
model, and give three measured numbers from one model and one question bank that prove it.

Diagnose position bias in a scoring procedure by comparing how often each option was
chosen against how often each option was correct, and compute the over-choice ratio.

Apply two standard debiasing fixes, scoring the option text with length normalisation and
taking a majority over cyclic rotations, and say what each one does and does not repair.

Compare two models on the same questions using a paired analysis, build the 95% interval
for the difference, and say in numbers how much the pairing bought you.

Run McNemar’s exact test on a two-by-two table of paired results, interpret a p-value of
0.0625 correctly, and explain why more questions, not a stronger claim, is the fix.

One model, one question bank, three defensible rules for marking it: 25.0%, 35.0%, 15.0%.
A twenty percentage point spread with nothing changed but the rule.

The first rule scored exactly chance, and the reason was that it was measuring a habit.
The model answered A on 16 of the 20 questions while the right answer was A twice.

Position bias is a symptom of a weak model, not a fixed tax. The gap between the naive
score and the debiased score is 10 points at 0.5B, 10 points at 1.5B, and 0 points at 3B.

A 25 point gap between two models can fail to be significant. On twenty questions, with
five disagreements all favouring the larger model, McNemar’s exact test returns p = 0.0625.

records.content:
Every technical term this chapter uses, defined before it is used. Read the table once now. You
do not have to memorise it; you have to know it exists, so that when a word appears in a
sentence you can come back and check it.

Term

What it means, in one line

scoring procedure

The complete rule for turning what a model produced into a right or a wrong.

answer extraction

The part of a scoring procedure that decides which option the model picked.

naive letter scoring

Asking which of the letter tokens A, B, C, D the model rates highest, and calling that its answer.

log-probability

The natural logarithm of a probability. A negative number. Bigger, meaning closer to zero, means more likely.

length normalisation

Dividing a total score by how many tokens it was added up over, so a long option is not punished for being long.

chance level

The score somebody would average by guessing at random. It belongs to a procedure, not to a question: with four options and one asking it is one in four, and Worked example 13.2 shows it changing when the procedure changes.

position bias

A scoring procedure rewarding an option for where it sits in the list rather than for being right.

over-choice ratio

How many times more often an option was chosen than an unbiased procedure would choose it.

cyclic rotation

Moving every option along one position and wrapping the last one round to the front.

majority vote

Asking the same question several times and keeping the answer that won most of the askings.

consistency (under rotation)

Whether the four rotations of one question all agreed with each other about whether the model was right.

debiasing gap

The naive score minus the debiased score, in percentage points.

paired comparison

Comparing two models question by question, because they answered the same questions.

unpaired comparison

Treating the two models’ scores as two separate samples, which throws the pairing away.

contingency table

A two-by-two count of how two models agreed and disagreed on the same items.

concordant pair

A question both models got right, or both got wrong.

discordant pair

A question exactly one of them got right.

standard deviation

How spread out a set of numbers is around their own average.

standard error

How much a measured number would wobble if you re-ran the whole measurement.

Wald interval

The textbook confidence interval: the measured number, plus or minus 1.96 standard errors. Built in 

Chapter 12, Definition 12.11, and known to be a poor fit at small sample sizes.

null hypothesis

The dull explanation a test tries to rule out: there is no real difference.

p-value

Assuming the null hypothesis is true, the chance of a result at least as lopsided as yours.

McNemar’s exact test

The significance test built for a paired yes-or-no comparison.

statistical significance

The verdict that a result is too lopsided to blame on sampling wobble, conventionally p < 0.05, which is read “p is less than nought point nought five”. See 

the toolkit on inequalities.

failure taxonomy

A naming of the kinds of failure a model system can have, so you can say which one you are looking at.

records.content:
Think about a driving test. Two examiners, one candidate, one car, one route. Examiner A marks
you on whether you completed the route safely. Examiner B marks you on a checklist of
forty-three specific manoeuvres. Examiner C sits in the back, says nothing, and marks you on
whether a passenger would feel comfortable.

You drove exactly the same way for all three. You could pass one and fail another. Nobody
cheated. The examiners measured different things and called them all “the driving test.”

Now change one word. Instead of a candidate, a language model. Instead of a route, twenty
multiple-choice questions. Instead of three examiners, three rules for reading the model’s
output and deciding which option it picked.

Here is the part that catches people. A model does not “pick” an option. A language model
produces a probability for every one of the 151,936 tokens it knows, for the next position in
the text. That is all it produces. Nowhere in that output is there a letter circled in pencil.
Somebody has to write a rule that turns 151,936 numbers into one of four letters, and that
somebody is you.

The rule is not a detail. The rule is half the measurement.

There are at least three sensible rules, and all three are in use in published research:

Ask about the letter. Show the model the question with its four options and see which
of the four letter tokens A, B, C and D it rates most likely to come next.

Ask about the words. Ignore the letters entirely. Score the actual text of each option,
then divide by how long that option is, and take the best.

Ask four times. Move the options around the page so that every option gets a turn in
every slot, ask the question once per arrangement, and keep the answer that wins the most
askings.

Every one of the three is defensible. You could write a paragraph defending any of them and a
reviewer would nod. They produce three different numbers on the same model and the same
questions, and the distance between the highest and the lowest is twenty percentage points.

That is the whole chapter in one paragraph. The rest is working out what to do about it.

records.content:
There is a formula for accuracy, and you met it in 

Chapter 11. This chapter writes it
again with one thing added: a symbol for the procedure. That single extra symbol is the idea of
the chapter made visible.

Formula 13.1: Accuracy under a scoring procedure

1. In words. To score a model, go through the questions one at a time. For each one, use
your rule to decide whether the model got it right, writing down a 1 if it did and a 0 if it did
not. Add up those ones and zeros, and divide by how many questions there were. The answer is the
share of questions the model got right according to that rule.

2. The formula.\hat{p}^{(g)} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} g(M, q_i)

3. The symbols.

Symbol

How to say it out loud

What it means

\hat{p}

“p hat”

the accuracy you measured. A number between 0 and 1

the hat, \hat{\phantom{p}}

“hat”

a mark meaning “this is something we measured, not something we know for certain”

g

“gee”

the scoring procedure: the complete rule for marking one answer

the raised (g) in \hat{p}^{(g)}

“under gee”

a label, not a power. It says which rule produced this accuracy

=

“equals”

the two sides are the same number

\dfrac{1}{n}

“one over en”

dividing by n after adding n things up is how you take an average

\dfrac{1}{n} and the sum written side by side

“times”

two things written next to each other with no sign between them means multiply them. See 

the toolkit on multiplication

the fraction bar

“divided by”

divide the top by the bottom

\sum_{i=1}^{n}

“the sum from i equals one to en”

add up what follows, once for each question, starting at question 1 and stopping at question n. The sign is a capital Greek S, and it is an instruction to add. See 

the toolkit on sigma notation

i

“eye”

a counter. i = 1 is the first question, i = 2 the second. See 

the toolkit on subscripts

n

“en”

how many questions there are. Here n = 20

M

“em”

the model being tested

q_i

“q sub i”

question number i

g(M, q_i)

“gee of em, q sub i”

what the rule g gives for model M on question i: 1 for right, 0 for wrong

4. Out loud. “The accuracy under a procedure is one over the number of questions, times the
sum, over every question, of what that procedure scored the model on that question.”

5. Worked, on the real run. The naive letter procedure marked 5 of the 20 questions right.
So fifteen of the g(M, q_i) values are 0 and five of them are 1.

Step 1, add up the twenty ones and zeros. Adding a 0 to a running total changes nothing, so
only the five ones move the total, and the sum is the same whatever order the questions came in.1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 5

Step 2, divide by the number of questions.\hat{p}^{(\text{letter})} = 5 \div 20 = 0.25

Step 3, turn that into a percentage by multiplying by 100. A percentage is a share written out of
a hundred instead of out of one, so multiplying by 100 is the whole of the conversion. See


the toolkit on percentages.0.25 \times 100 = 25.0\%

Now the option-text procedure, which marked 7 right.\hat{p}^{(\text{text})} = 7 \div 20 = 0.35, \qquad 0.35 \times 100 = 35.0\%

And the rotation procedure, which marked 3 right.\hat{p}^{(\text{rotation})} = 3 \div 20 = 0.15, \qquad 0.15 \times 100 = 15.0\%

Step 4, the distance from the highest to the lowest.35.0 - 15.0 = 20.0 \text{ percentage points}

6. Check it. Four checks, and they catch almost every slip anybody makes here.

Your accuracy must land between 0 and 1. If you get 1.75 you divided by the wrong thing.

Multiply your accuracy back by n and you must get a whole number, because you cannot get
half a question right. 0.35 \times 20 = 7, a whole number, so that one is sound.

None of the three numbers is finished until it carries an interval beside it. A measured
accuracy is a share taken from a sample of twenty questions, so it wobbles, and


Chapter 12 measured that wobble: the 25.0% comes with a 95% interval running from
6.0% to 44.0%. Write the interval down every time you write the number down. This chapter
prints the three bare percentages over and over because they are the thing being argued about,
and each time you read one, read the interval back onto it.

And the answer to “which is the model’s score” is not one of these three numbers. It is the
question “under which procedure?”

Definition 13.1: Scoring procedure

A scoring procedure is the complete rule for turning what a model produced into a right or a
wrong. It includes how the question is written into a prompt, how the model’s output is read,
how ties are broken, and what counts as correct. Two people who agree on the model, agree on the
questions, and disagree on the procedure will disagree on the score.

Definition 13.2: Answer extraction

Answer extraction is the part of a scoring procedure that decides which option the model
picked. A model outputs probabilities over tokens, never a circled letter, so extraction is
always a decision somebody made. It is not something you read off.

The three accuracies are in the file. Pull them out, turn them into counts of questions, and
measure the spread.# Pull the three accuracies out of the file, one line each.
naive_accuracy = three_procedures["naive_accuracy"]
option_text_accuracy = three_procedures["option_text_accuracy"]
rotation_accuracy = three_procedures["rotation_majority_accuracy"]

# Turn each proportion into a count of questions. "7 of 20" is easier to picture than "0.35".
naive_correct = round(naive_accuracy * question_count)
option_text_correct = round(option_text_accuracy * question_count)
rotation_correct = round(rotation_accuracy * question_count)

print("procedure 1, the letter      :", round(naive_accuracy * 100, 1), "percent  =", naive_correct, "of", question_count)
print("procedure 2, the option text :", round(option_text_accuracy * 100, 1), "percent  =", option_text_correct, "of", question_count)
print("procedure 3, four rotations  :", round(rotation_accuracy * 100, 1), "percent  =", rotation_correct, "of", question_count)

# The distance from the highest of the three to the lowest, in percentage points.
highest_accuracy = max(naive_accuracy, option_text_accuracy, rotation_accuracy)
lowest_accuracy = min(naive_accuracy, option_text_accuracy, rotation_accuracy)
spread_in_points = round((highest_accuracy - lowest_accuracy) * 100, 1)

print("highest of the three:", round(highest_accuracy * 100, 1), "percent")
print("lowest of the three :", round(lowest_accuracy * 100, 1), "percent")
print("spread              :", spread_in_points, "percentage points")

Output:procedure 1, the letter      : 25.0 percent  = 5 of 20
procedure 2, the option text : 35.0 percent  = 7 of 20
procedure 3, four rotations  : 15.0 percent  = 3 of 20
highest of the three: 35.0 percent
lowest of the three : 15.0 percent
spread              : 20.0 percentage points

Several things in that block are worth naming, because they come back all chapter.

three_procedures["naive_accuracy"] reaches into the loaded file and takes out the value stored
under the label naive_accuracy. The square brackets with a word inside them are how you ask a
Python dictionary for one of its values. A dictionary is a bundle of labelled values, and it
is how these result files are shaped.

round(naive_accuracy * 100, 1) does two things in one step. It multiplies the proportion by 100
to turn it into a percentage, and the 1 says keep one digit after the decimal point. Without
the rounding you would sometimes see 35.000000000000004 on your screen, which is a fact about
how computers store decimals and is taken apart in 

Chapter 6.

max(...) and min(...) give the largest and smallest of the numbers you hand them.

Now read the output slowly. Five, seven and three. Out of twenty. Those are the raw counts,
and they are so small that the difference between the best and worst procedure is four questions.
Four questions moved, and a reader of the headline number would come away with either “this
model is worse than guessing” or “this model beats guessing by ten points.”

Both sentences would be true. Neither is a fact about the model.

Worked example 13.1: Turning a count into a percentage, and back

The option-text procedure got 7 of 20 right. Show that this is 35%, and then go the other way.

Forwards. Divide the number right by the number asked.

7 \div 20 = 0.35

Multiply by 100 to get a percentage.

0.35 \times 100 = 35, so 35.0%.

Backwards. Somebody tells you a model scored 35% on a twenty-question bank. How many did it
get right?

Turn the percentage into a decimal by dividing by 100.

35 \div 100 = 0.35

Multiply by the number of questions.

0.35 \times 20 = 7 questions.

The check. The answer to the backwards direction must be a whole number. If somebody reports
37% on a twenty-question bank, then 0.37 \times 20 = 7.4 questions, which is impossible. Either
the bank was not twenty questions or the number was rounded from something else. On a
twenty-question bank the only scores that can exist are multiples of 5 percentage points: 0%, 5%,
10%, and so on up to 100%. There are exactly 21 of them. A benchmark that small cannot express
“41%” at all.

records.content:
Here is a habit worth building, and it costs nothing.

When you see a score on a multiple-choice test, work out what a person who knew nothing would
average, and compare. On a four-option test, somebody who closed their eyes and pointed would
get about one question in four. One in four is 25%.

The naive letter procedure scored the 0.5B model at 25.0%.

Not near 25%. Not 24% or 26%. Exactly the number a coin-flipping, dice-rolling, eyes-closed
guesser would average. Five questions out of twenty, which is precisely 20 \div 4.

There are two possible readings, and a statistician’s instinct is to check the second one first.

Reading one: the model knows nothing. That is entirely possible. It is a 494,032,768
parameter model, which is small, and the questions are about statistics. A model that knows
nothing would score around chance. This reading is unremarkable and might well be true.

Reading two: the measuring instrument is broken. A thermometer that reads 20 degrees in a
freezer and 20 degrees in an oven is not telling you the freezer and the oven are the same
temperature. It is telling you the thermometer is not connected to anything. A scoring procedure
that returns exactly the guessing rate might be measuring something that has nothing to do with
whether the model knows statistics.

Reading two is worth checking first for a simple reason: if it is right, reading one has not
been tested at all. You cannot conclude the model is ignorant from an instrument that is not
plugged in.

A score sitting exactly on chance is not a result. It is a question. And the question is not
“how much does this model know?” It is “what was that procedure actually measuring?”

This chapter answers it, and the answer is worse than you would guess.

Two small formulas, and both of them are arithmetic rather than measurement. That distinction
matters and the figures in this chapter keep it visible: the chance level is drawn as a
reference, never as a bar of measured data.

Formula 13.2: The chance level on a multiple-choice question

1. In words. If every question has the same number of options and exactly one of them is
right, then somebody guessing at random gets one question right for every however-many options
there are. The share they get right is one divided by the number of options.

2. The formula.c = \frac{1}{k}

3. The symbols.

the toolkit on the fraction bar

how many options each question has. Here k = 4

4. Out loud. “The chance level is one divided by the number of options.”

5. Worked, with four options.c = \frac{1}{4} = 1 \div 4 = 0.25

As a percentage, 0.25 \times 100 = 25.0\%.

And with other option counts, so the pattern is visible:

6. Check it. The chance level must fall between 0 and 1, and it must shrink as you add
options, because more options means guessing gets harder. If your chance level went up when you
added an option, you divided the wrong way round. And note what c is not: it is not a
measurement of any model. It is arithmetic about the test. No model was run to produce 0.25.

One limit on this formula, and it matters later. Formula 13.2 assumes the procedure asks each
question once and takes the answer. A procedure that asks four times and requires three hits
has a different and much lower chance level, and Worked example 13.2 in section 13.5 computes it.
So 1 \div k is the chance level of a procedure, not of a question.

Formula 13.3: How many questions a guesser gets right

1. In words. Multiply the share a guesser averages by the number of questions on the test.
That tells you roughly how many questions a guesser gets right.

2. The formula.E = c \times n = \frac{n}{k}

3. The symbols.

4. Out loud. “The expected number right is the chance level times the number of questions,
which is the number of questions divided by the number of options.”

5. Worked, on this bank.

Route one, through the chance level.E = 0.25 \times 20 = 5

Route two, the short way.E = \frac{20}{4} = 20 \div 4 = 5

Both routes give 5, as they must. And the naive procedure’s measured result was 5 questions
right. The difference is 5 - 5 = 0 questions.

6. Check it. E can never be bigger than n; you cannot expect more right answers than
there are questions. Here is the important caution, though: “expected 5” does not mean a guesser
always gets exactly 5. A guesser could get 2, or 9. 

Chapter 12 measured that wobble
for you: on twenty questions, a measured 25.0% carries a 95% interval from 6.0% to 44.0%. So the
fact that the naive procedure landed exactly on 5 is a coincidence of this particular run, and
the argument of this section does not depend on it being exact. Landing anywhere near chance
would raise the same question.

records.content:
Here is how the naive procedure works, in full, with nothing hidden.

You build a prompt. It holds the question, then the four options each on its own line with its
letter in front, then the word Answer: and nothing after it. You hand that to the model and
ask for the probabilities of the next token. Out come 151,936 numbers. You ignore 151,932 of
them. You keep the four belonging to the tokens A, B, C and D, and whichever of those
four is biggest is recorded as the model’s answer.

Now ask a question nobody normally asks. Across all twenty questions, how often did each
letter win?

If the procedure were measuring knowledge, and the model had some, the answers would follow the
answer key, roughly. If the model knew nothing at all and was genuinely undecided, the four
letters would come up about five times each. Either way you would expect some spread.

Here is what happened.

The model answered A on 16 of the 20 questions. B twice. C never once. D twice.

And the correct answers in the bank are spread B eight times, C eight times, D twice, A twice.

Put those two lines side by side and the whole thing falls apart. The model reached for the
letter A whether the question was about the mean of four numbers or about what a p-value is. The
answer key rewarded A on two questions out of twenty. So the procedure gave the model credit
almost by accident, on whichever questions happened to have A as the answer, plus a few lucky
landings elsewhere.

That is what 25.0% was made of. Not knowledge. A habit.

And notice the direction the bias points. The letter C is the right answer on eight of the
twenty questions, which is 40% of the bank, and the model chose C zero times. A procedure
that can never select 40% of the correct answers has a ceiling on it that has nothing to do with
what the model knows.

This has a name. When a scoring procedure rewards an option for where it sits rather than for
being right, that is position bias. It is a bias in the statistical sense: a systematic push
in a fixed direction, which more data does not remove. Ask this model two thousand questions
instead of twenty and it will still reach for A. A bigger sample makes a random wobble smaller.
It does nothing to a systematic push.

The arithmetic here is small on purpose. The point is not the difficulty; it is that nobody
looks.

Formula 13.4: The over-choice ratio for one option

1. In words. Count how many times a scoring procedure landed on one particular option.
Compare that with how many times it would have landed there if it had no preference between
positions. Divide the first number by the second. An answer of 1 means no preference. An answer
bigger than 1 means the procedure is over-choosing that option.

2. The formula.R_j = \frac{m_j}{E} = \frac{m_j}{n/k}

3. The symbols.

Symbol

How to say it out loud

What it means

R_j

“R sub j”

the over-choice ratio for option j. The answer

j

“jay”

which option we are asking about. j = A, or j = B, and so on

=

“equals”

the two sides are the same number

m_j

“m sub j”

how many times the procedure chose option j, counted across all the questions

the fraction bar

“divided by”

divide the top by the bottom

E

“ee”

the expected count from Formula 13.3: n/k, how often an unbiased procedure lands on each option

n

“en”

the number of questions, 20

k

“kay”

the number of options per question, 4

4. Out loud. “The over-choice ratio for an option is the number of times that option was
chosen, divided by the number of times a procedure with no position preference would have
chosen it.”

5. Worked, on the real run.

Step 1, work out the expected count. Every question has four options, and there are twenty
questions.E = \frac{n}{k} = \frac{20}{4} = 5

Step 2, the ratio for each letter. The chosen counts are A 16, B 2, C 0, D 2.R_A = \frac{16}{5} = 16 \div 5 = 3.2R_B = \frac{2}{5} = 2 \div 5 = 0.4R_C = \frac{0}{5} = 0 \div 5 = 0.0R_D = \frac{2}{5} = 2 \div 5 = 0.4

Step 3, read them. Option A was chosen 3.2 times more often than an unbiased procedure
would. Option C was chosen 0.0 times as often, which is to say never.

Step 4, the share of all answers taken by A.\frac{16}{20} = 16 \div 20 = 0.8, \qquad 0.8 \times 100 = 80.0\%

Four fifths of every answer this procedure produced was the letter A.

6. Check it. The chosen counts have to add to the number of questions, because every
question got exactly one answer: 16 + 2 + 0 + 2 = 20. ✅ If yours do not add to n, you
mis-tallied.

And the ratios have to average to 1 across the options, because the total is fixed. Check:
3.2 + 0.4 + 0.0 + 0.4 = 4.0, and 4.0 \div 4 = 1.0. ✅ If your ratios average to something
other than 1, you used the wrong expected count.

Definition 13.3: Position bias

Position bias is the tendency of a scoring procedure to reward an option for where it sits
in the list rather than for being correct. It is a statistical bias: a systematic error in one
fixed direction, which does not shrink as you collect more data. The standard fixes are to score
the option text instead of the position label, or to move the options around and take a majority.

Definition 13.4: Bias, in the statistical sense

This book uses the word bias in two unrelated senses and always says which.

Statistical bias is an instrument that reads wrong in a fixed direction. A bathroom scale
that adds four pounds to everybody is biased. Weighing yourself a thousand times does not fix it.

Fairness bias, the subject of 

Chapter 14, is a system working less well for some
groups of people than others. It is a social and ethical claim.

They are not the same thing and neither one implies the other. Everything in this chapter is the
statistical sense.



Figure 1:The right panel is the one this chapter is about. Each bar is one of the four options, and
its height is how many times out of twenty the naive letter procedure recorded that option as the
model’s answer. The dashed grey line sits at 5, which is what a procedure with no position
preference would average on each option, from Formula 13.3. Option A reaches 16, which is 3.2
times the line. Option C does not appear at all, and C was the correct answer on eight of the
twenty questions. The left panel belongs to 

Chapter 3 and is included because the two
panels were drawn by the same script, lab/make_figures.py, from
lab/out/we3_params_quant.json and lab/out/we6b_eval_debiased.json.

The for loop repeats its indented lines once for each item in the list ["A", "B", "C", "D"].
On the first pass one_letter holds "A", on the second "B", and so on. str(...) turns a
number into text so it can be glued to other text with +, and .rjust(2) pads a short piece

winner, then checks each letter in turn and moves the title whenever it finds a bigger count.

the thing you can read out loud.

Now the table. Read it column by column, not row by row.

Column two is what the procedure produced. Column three is the answer key. They have almost
nothing to do with each other. The procedure’s favourite option is the key’s rarest. The key’s
most common options, B and C with eight each, were chosen twice and never.

would average. The gap between column two and column four is the bias, in questions.

A last observation, and it is the one that should make you uncomfortable. If this run had been a
paper, the sentence in the abstract would have been “the model performs at chance on
undergraduate statistics.” That sentence is well formed, it is supported by the number, and it
would survive review. It is also not supported by anything that happened, because the instrument
that produced it was measuring a preference for a letter.

records.content:
The diagnosis suggests its own repair. The trouble came from asking about the letters. So stop
asking about the letters.

Instead of “which of A, B, C or D do you rate highest”, ask something the letters play no part
in. Take the prompt, and for each option in turn, stick the actual words of that option on
the end and ask the model how likely that continuation was. Then take whichever option the model
found most likely.

Question 1 of the bank is “The mean of 2, 4, 4, 6 is:” with options 3, 4, 5 and 6. Under this
procedure the model is not being asked about the letter B. It is being asked how likely the text
4 is to follow the question. The position of 4 on the page has stopped mattering, because
the position is no longer part of what you score.

There is one complication, and it is the interesting part.

Options are not all the same length. Question 14 asks what a p-value is, and one option reads
“The effect size”, three words, while another reads “The probability of data this extreme if the
null is true”, eleven words. Every extra token you score is another number below zero being
added to the total. A longer option accumulates a worse total merely for being longer, even
when the model likes every word of it.

So a procedure that took the best total would pick short options almost every time. That is a
new bias, substituted for the old one.

The repair for the repair is to divide by the length. Instead of the total score for an option,
take the average score per token: the total divided by how many tokens the option took. Now
a long option and a short option are on the same footing, because both are being judged on how
good their typical token was rather than on how many tokens they had.

That step has a name, length normalisation, and it is one line of code and a genuinely
important idea. Whenever you compare totals built from different numbers of pieces, you have to
decide whether you are comparing totals or averages, and the two can rank things in opposite
orders.

records.content:
Formula 13.5: The length-normalised score of an option

1. In words. Take one option. The model gives a log-probability for each of its tokens. Add
those up, then divide by how many tokens there were. The result is the option’s typical
per-token score, and it does not get worse merely because the option is long.

2. The formula.\bar{\ell}_j = \frac{1}{L_j} \sum_{t=1}^{L_j} \ln p_{j,t}

3. The symbols.

Symbol

How to say it out loud

What it means

\bar{\ell}_j

“ell bar sub j”

the answer: option j’s average log-probability per token. A negative number

the bar over the \ell

“bar”

a mark meaning “this is an average”

\ell

“ell”

the letter L in a script style, used here for “log-probability”

j

“jay”

which option. j = A, j = B, and so on

=

“equals”

the two sides are the same number

\dfrac{1}{L_j}

“one over L sub j”

dividing by L_j after adding L_j things is how you take an average

the fraction bar

“divided by”

divide the top by the bottom. See 

the toolkit on the fraction bar

\dfrac{1}{L_j} and the sum written side by side

“times”

two things written next to each other with no sign between them means multiply them. See 

the toolkit on multiplication

L_j

“L sub j”

how many tokens option j is made of

\sum_{t=1}^{L_j}

“the sum from t equals one to L sub j”

add up what follows, once for each token of the option. See 

the toolkit on sigma notation

t

“tee”

a counter over the tokens of this option. t=1 is its first token

\ln

“ell en”, or “natural log”

the natural logarithm. It turns a probability between 0 and 1 into a negative number, and keeps the ranking identical. See 

the toolkit on logarithms

p_{j,t}

“p sub j comma t”

the probability the model gave to token t of option j

\ln p_{j,t}

“ell en of p sub j comma t”

the log-probability of that one token. Always negative, because probabilities are below 1

4. Out loud. “The normalised score of an option is one over its number of tokens, times the
sum of the log-probabilities of all its tokens.”

5. Worked. These seven numbers are made up for practice; no model produced them.

Two options. The short one is two tokens with log-probabilities -1.2 and -0.9. The long one
is five tokens with log-probabilities -1.2, -0.9, -1.1, -0.8 and -1.0. That is two
numbers plus five numbers, seven invented values in all.

Step 1, add up the short option’s log-probabilities.-1.2 + (-0.9) = -2.1

Step 2, add up the long option’s.-1.2 + (-0.9) + (-1.1) + (-0.8) + (-1.0) = -5.0

Step 3, compare the totals. -2.1 against -5.0. Since -2.1 is closer to zero, it is the
larger number, so on totals the short option wins by a distance.

Step 4, divide each by its number of tokens.\bar{\ell}_{\text{short}} = \frac{-2.1}{2} = -2.1 \div 2 = -1.05\bar{\ell}_{\text{long}} = \frac{-5.0}{5} = -5.0 \div 5 = -1.00

Step 5, compare again. -1.00 is closer to zero than -1.05, so the long option now wins.

The ranking flipped. Nothing about the model’s opinion changed between step 3 and step 5. The
only thing that changed was whether you compared totals or averages.

6. Check it. Every log-probability must be negative or zero, because every probability is
between 0 and 1 and the logarithm of a number below 1 is negative. If one of yours is positive,
you took the log of something that was not a probability.

The average must land between the smallest and the largest of the values you averaged. Here the
long option’s values run from -1.2 to -0.8, and -1.00 sits inside that range. ✅ If your
average falls outside the range of the numbers that made it, you divided by the wrong count.

Definition 13.5: Length normalisation

Length normalisation is dividing a total that was built up from several pieces by the number
of pieces, so that things made of different numbers of pieces can be compared fairly. Here it
turns a total log-probability into a per-token average, so a long answer is not penalised for
being long.

The loops below add up two short lists by hand, one number at a time, so you can see what the
\sum in Formula 13.5 does. Then the last two lines print the real measured result.# A made-up example, invented for practice, to show what dividing by the length does.
# These log-probabilities are not measurements. Nothing above this line produced them.
short_option_log_probabilities = [-1.2, -0.9]
long_option_log_probabilities = [-1.2, -0.9, -1.1, -0.8, -1.0]

# Add up the short option's log-probabilities with an explicit loop.
short_option_total = 0.0
for one_value in short_option_log_probabilities:
    short_option_total = short_option_total + one_value

# Add up the long option's log-probabilities the same way.
long_option_total = 0.0
for one_value in long_option_log_probabilities:
    long_option_total = long_option_total + one_value

print("short option, total    :", round(short_option_total, 4), "over", len(short_option_log_probabilities), "tokens")
print("long option, total     :", round(long_option_total, 4), "over", len(long_option_log_probabilities), "tokens")
print("short option, per token:", round(short_option_total / len(short_option_log_probabilities), 4))
print("long option, per token :", round(long_option_total / len(long_option_log_probabilities), 4))

# Now the real measurement, from the file.
option_text_counts = three_procedures["option_text_counts"]
print("real run, option-text procedure:", round(option_text_accuracy * 100, 1), "percent")
print("real run, which positions it chose:", option_text_counts)

Output:short option, total    : -2.1 over 2 tokens
long option, total     : -5.0 over 5 tokens
short option, per token: -1.05
long option, per token : -1.0
real run, option-text procedure: 35.0 percent
real run, which positions it chose: {'A': 7, 'B': 11, 'C': 2, 'D': 0}

short_option_total = 0.0 sets up an empty running total before the loop starts. Then
short_option_total = short_option_total + one_value adds the next number to it. Read that line
right to left: take what the total currently holds, add the new value, store the answer back
under the same name. A loop that does this is an accumulator, and it is how every \sum in
this book is carried out in code. len(...) counts how many items are in a list.

Now the measured result, and it comes in two halves.

The good half. The score went from 25.0% to 35.0%. Seven questions out of twenty instead of
five. That is two more questions, and it is ten percentage points above the chance level.

The half nobody prints. Look at where this procedure’s answers landed: A seven times, B
eleven times, C twice, D never. Against an answer key of A two, B eight, C eight, D two.

It is a different bias. It is not a smaller one.

This procedure now over-chooses B, by a ratio of 11 \div 5 = 2.2. It still barely touches C,
choosing it twice where the key rewards it eight times. It never once selects D. An unbiased
procedure would land on each option about five times; this one produced 7, 11, 2 and 0.

So the honest report on fix one is: the score improved, and the instrument is still bent. It is
bent in a new direction, which makes it harder to notice, because 35% does not sit suspiciously
on the chance line the way 25% did.

That is the most dangerous kind of broken instrument: the one whose reading looks plausible.

records.content:
The second fix goes at the problem from the other end, and it is the more powerful of the two.

If you suspect the model is answering based on where an option sits, then move the options and
see whether its answer follows. That is all. It is exactly what a careful teacher does when they
suspect a student copied: they hand out the same test with the questions in a different order.

Here is the procedure in full. Take one question. Ask it four times. On the first asking, leave
the options where they are. On the second, move every option up one place and wrap the top one
round to the bottom, so what was option B is now option A. On the third, move them again. On the
fourth, again. After four moves every option has occupied every position exactly once. That
sliding-and-wrapping move is called a cyclic rotation.

Each time, you write down whether the model landed on the correct option, wherever the correct
option happens to be sitting now. Then you take the majority: if the model was right on at
least three of the four askings, the question counts as correct.

A model that knows an answer will follow that answer around the page. If it knows the mean of
2, 4, 4 and 6 is 4, it should select 4 whether 4 is sitting in slot A, B, C or D. A model
that is reaching for a position will be right exactly once in four, because the correct option
passes through its favourite slot exactly once during the rotation.

Read that last sentence again, because it is the sharp edge of this section. A model that
always answers A scores one out of four on every single question under rotation, and one out
of four is below the three-out-of-four majority, so it fails every question. Rotation does not
soften position bias. It removes the reward for it entirely.

Applied to all twenty questions, the score came out at 15.0%. Three questions of twenty.
Below the naive 25.0%. Below the option-text 35.0%.

Here is where you have to be careful, and it is the chapter’s own lesson turned back on the
chapter. It is tempting to write “and 15.0% is below the chance level of 25%.” That sentence is
wrong. The 25% chance level belongs to a procedure that asks each question once. This
procedure asks each question four times and demands at least three hits, which is a much harder
target for a guesser. A guesser facing this rule averages about 5.1%, not 25%, and Worked
example 13.2 does that arithmetic in full. So 15.0% is in fact above chance for the
procedure that produced it.

Changing the rule changed the chance level too. A chance level is a property of a procedure, in
exactly the way a score is, and comparing a score from one procedure against a chance level
computed for another is the same mistake in a smaller costume.

And the second number this procedure produces is the one that ends the argument. Of the twenty
questions, the four rotations agreed with each other on exactly one.

records.content:
Two formulas and one worked example. The first formula says where the correct answer moves to.
The second is the punchline. The worked example settles what a guesser would score under this
rule, which is the line the 15.0% has to be read against.

Formula 13.6: Where the correct answer sits after a rotation

1. In words. When you slide all the options up by some number of places and wrap the ones
that fall off the top around to the bottom, the correct answer moves up by the same number of
places, and it wraps around too. To find where it landed, subtract the number of places you
slid, and if the answer goes below zero, add the number of options back on.

2. The formula.g_r = (g - r) \bmod k

3. The symbols.

Symbol

How to say it out loud

What it means

g_r

“g sub r”

the answer: which position the correct option occupies after rotation r

g

“gee”

which position the correct option started in. Counting from 0, so position 0 is option A, position 1 is option B, position 2 is C, position 3 is D. This is not the g of Formula 13.1, which stood for a scoring procedure. A letter gets re-used for a new job now and then, and when this book does that it says so

r

“arr”

how many places you slid the options. r = 0 means no slide

=

“equals”

the two sides are the same number

-

“minus”

subtract

the round brackets, (\;)

“bracket, close bracket”

do what is inside them first. So (g - r) \bmod k means subtract first, then take the remainder

\bmod

“mod”, short for “modulo”

the remainder after dividing. It is what makes the wrapping happen

k

“kay”

how many options there are, 4

A note on “mod”, which is one of the two unfamiliar symbols in this chapter. The other is
the “choose” sign in Formula 13.11, and it gets the same treatment when it arrives. \bmod means
“take the remainder after dividing”. So 7 \bmod 4 = 3, because 7 divided by 4 is 1 with 3 left
over. It is the arithmetic of a clock face: five hours after ten o’clock is three o’clock, because
15 \bmod 12 = 3. When the number underneath is negative, keep adding k until it is not:
-1 \bmod 4 = 3, because -1 + 4 = 3.

4. Out loud. “The correct position after a rotation is the starting position minus the
rotation number, with the remainder taken after dividing by the number of options.”

5. Worked, on question 1 of the bank. The question is “The mean of 2, 4, 4, 6 is:” and the
options are 3, 4, 5, 6. The correct answer is 4, sitting in position 1, which is option B.

Rotation r = 0. No slide.g_0 = (1 - 0) \bmod 4 = 1 \bmod 4 = 1 \rightarrow \text{option B}

Rotation r = 1. The options become 4, 5, 6, 3.g_1 = (1 - 1) \bmod 4 = 0 \bmod 4 = 0 \rightarrow \text{option A}

Rotation r = 2. The options become 5, 6, 3, 4.g_2 = (1 - 2) \bmod 4 = (-1) \bmod 4 = 3 \rightarrow \text{option D}

That third line is where the wrapping shows. 1 - 2 = -1, and -1 + 4 = 3, so the correct
answer is now option D.

Rotation r = 3. The options become 6, 3, 4, 5.g_3 = (1 - 3) \bmod 4 = (-2) \bmod 4 = 2 \rightarrow \text{option C}

6. Check it. Across the four rotations the correct answer must visit all four positions
exactly once. Here it visited B, A, D, C. ✅ Every letter appears once. If one letter appears
twice, you have a mistake in the mod arithmetic, and the usual cause is not adding k back on
when the subtraction went negative.

Formula 13.7: The consistency rate under rotation

1. In words. Count how many questions the four rotations agreed on, meaning the model was
right all four times or wrong all four times. Divide by the number of questions. That gives you
the share of questions where the model behaved the same way no matter where the options sat.

2. The formula.\hat{c} = \frac{u}{n}

3. The symbols.

Symbol

How to say it out loud

What it means

\hat{c}

“c hat”

the answer: the consistency rate, between 0 and 1. This is not the c of Formula 13.2, which was the chance level. The hat is the clue: this one was measured

the hat

“hat”

a mark meaning “measured, not known for certain”

=

“equals”

the two sides are the same number

u

“you”

how many questions the four rotations agreed on: right four times, or wrong four times

the fraction bar

“divided by”

divide the top by the bottom

n

“en”

the number of questions, 20

4. Out loud. “The consistency rate is the number of questions the rotations agreed on,
divided by the number of questions.”

5. Worked, on the real run. The lab measured u = 1 out of n = 20.\hat{c} = \frac{1}{20} = 1 \div 20 = 0.05, \qquad 0.05 \times 100 = 5.0\%

Now work out what a position-locked model would score, so you have something to compare against.
Suppose a model always picks position A, whatever the question says. On each question the correct
answer passes through position A exactly once in the four rotations, so the model is right once
and wrong three times. That is neither four-out-of-four nor zero-out-of-four, so the rotations
disagree, and the question is not consistent.\hat{c}_{\text{always-A}} = \frac{0}{20} = 0.0

And a model that genuinely knows the material is right on all four rotations of every question it
knows, so those questions are consistent.

So the consistency rate runs from 0, for a model that is purely following positions, up towards
1, for a model that is actually reading the options. The measured 0.05 sits almost at the bottom
of that range.

6. Check it. u cannot exceed n, so \hat{c} cannot exceed 1. And here is a check on your
understanding rather than your arithmetic: a low consistency rate is not the same as a low
score. A model could be consistently wrong on every question, always picking the same incorrect
option, and score 0% with a consistency rate of 1.0. That would tell you it had a firm, wrong
opinion. A consistency rate near zero tells you something different and worse: the answers are
not opinions at all.

Worked example 13.2: The chance level of the rotation procedure

Formula 13.2 said the chance level with four options is 1 \div 4 = 0.25. That was for a
procedure that asks each question once. The rotation procedure asks four times and requires at
least three hits. Work out what a guesser averages under that rule.

Step 1, the chance of one asking. Four options, one right, so 1 \div 4 = 0.25, and the
chance of missing is 1 - 0.25 = 0.75.

Step 2, list the outcomes that count as correct. The rule needs 3 or 4 hits out of 4. So
there are two outcomes to add up: exactly 3 hits, and exactly 4 hits.

Step 3, exactly 4 hits. All four askings have to land. Multiply 0.25 by itself four times.0.25 \times 0.25 = 0.06250.0625 \times 0.25 = 0.0156250.015625 \times 0.25 = 0.00390625

Step 4, exactly 3 hits. Three askings land and one misses, which is
0.25 \times 0.25 \times 0.25 \times 0.75.0.25 \times 0.25 \times 0.25 = 0.0156250.015625 \times 0.75 = 0.01171875

But the miss could be any one of the four askings, so there are four ways this can happen. That
count is the “choose” sign of Formula 13.11 doing a small job: \binom{4}{3} = 4.4 \times 0.01171875 = 0.046875

Step 5, add the two outcomes.0.046875 + 0.00390625 = 0.05078125

Step 6, as a percentage.0.05078125 \times 100 = 5.078125\%, \text{ which rounds to } 5.1\%

The check. The answer has to be smaller than the single-asking chance level of 25%, because
the rule asks for three hits where before it asked for one, and asking for more cannot make
guessing easier. And 5.1% is smaller than 25%. ✅ A second check: written as a fraction the
answer is 13 \div 256, and 256 = 2^8, which is a whole number of halvings, so the arithmetic
is exact rather than rounded.

One assumption, stated. Steps 3 and 4 multiply the four askings together, and multiplying
probabilities like that assumes the four askings do not influence each other. For a guesser that
is true. For a real model it is not: a model with a habit will lean the same way every time. So
5.1% is the chance level for guessing, which is what a chance level is for, and it is not a
prediction about any particular model.

What it means. The measured 15.0% is about three times the 5.1% a guesser would average
under this rule. Read against its own chance level, the rotation score is not a chance result.
It is a low score, from a weak model, on a procedure that no longer pays for a position habit.
The rotation procedure is also the one the two-model comparison in section 13.7 runs on, so
knowing where its chance line sits is worth the two minutes.

Read the definition of a metric before you quote it

The consistency count in lab/out/we6b_eval_debiased.json counts a question as consistent when
the four rotations agreed on the verdict: right all four times, or wrong all four times. You
can read that in the script, lab/we6b_eval_debiased.py, in the line if sum(votes) in (0, 4).

That is subtly different from “gave the same answer all four times”. A model could be wrong four
times while giving four different wrong answers, and this measure would count it as consistent.

The distinction does not change the conclusion here, because of the argument worked in Formula
13.7: a model locked onto one position is right exactly once in four and therefore counts as
inconsistent under this measure. So a consistency of 1 out of 20 is, if anything, harsher on
the model than the looser phrase would be.

This point belongs in a chapter about measuring your measurement, and it applies to this book
as much as to anyone else’s. A metric is a procedure. Read its definition before you quote its
number, including when the number is ours.

Definition 13.6: Cyclic rotation

A cyclic rotation slides every option along by a fixed number of places and wraps the ones
that fall off the end back round to the start. After k rotations of a k-option question,
every option has occupied every position exactly once.

Definition 13.7: Majority vote

A majority vote asks the same question several times under different conditions and keeps
the answer that won more than half the askings. Here, a question counts as correct when the model
landed on the right option in at least 3 of the 4 rotations.

# Question 1 of the bank, with its four options in their printed order.
option_list = ["3", "4", "5", "6"]
letter_list = ["A", "B", "C", "D"]

# The right answer is 4, which sits in position 1, because Python counts from 0.
correct_position = 1

for rotation_number in range(option_count):
    # Rotate left: take everything from rotation_number onward, then everything before it.
    rotated_options = option_list[rotation_number:] + option_list[:rotation_number]
    # Work out where the right answer has moved to. The % sign is remainder after division.
    new_correct_position = (correct_position - rotation_number) % option_count
    print("rotation", rotation_number, rotated_options,
          " the right answer is now option", letter_list[new_correct_position])

# The two measured results of doing this to all 20 questions.
consistent_questions = three_procedures["fully_consistent_questions"]
print("score under majority-of-four-rotations:", round(rotation_accuracy * 100, 1), "percent")
print("questions where all four rotations agreed:", consistent_questions, "of", question_count)
print("that is", round(100 * consistent_questions / question_count, 1), "percent consistent")

Output:rotation 0 ['3', '4', '5', '6']  the right answer is now option B
rotation 1 ['4', '5', '6', '3']  the right answer is now option A
rotation 2 ['5', '6', '3', '4']  the right answer is now option D
rotation 3 ['6', '3', '4', '5']  the right answer is now option C
score under majority-of-four-rotations: 15.0 percent
questions where all four rotations agreed: 1 of 20
that is 5.0 percent consistent

Three pieces of Python are new here.

option_list[rotation_number:] takes a slice of a list: everything from that position to the
end. option_list[:rotation_number] takes everything before that position. Gluing the two
together with + performs the rotation. On the second pass, rotation_number is 1, so the first
slice is ['4','5','6'], the second is ['3'], and together they make ['4','5','6','3'].

% between two whole numbers is the remainder after division, which is the \bmod from Formula
13.6. In Python, (1 - 2) % 4 gives 3, with the wrapping already handled for you.

range(option_count) produces the numbers 0, 1, 2, 3. It stops before the number you give
it, which catches everybody once.

Now the output. The first four lines show the correct answer visiting B, A, D and C, one position
per rotation, exactly as Formula 13.6 predicted.

The last three lines are the real result, and the middle one is the most important number in this
chapter.

One question out of twenty.

On nineteen of the twenty questions, moving the options around changed whether the model was
right. Its answers were not opinions about statistics that happened to be wrong. They were
responses to the layout of the page.

At this point you have three numbers, 25.0%, 35.0% and 15.0%, and you could defend any one of
them in writing. But the consistency count tells you what the honest report is, and it is not a
number at all. It is a sentence: this model does not know this material, and a single figure
should not have been printed.

That sentence is worth more than any of the three percentages. It is also the sentence that never
appears on a leaderboard.

Everything in sections 13.1 through 13.5 is in the page below, and you can move between the two
views with the slider. View 0 puts the three procedures side by side against the chance level.
View 1 is the diagnosis: for each letter, how often the model chose it against how often it was
the right answer.

Try it 13.1: Predict before you look

Before you move the slider, answer these three on paper.

A model that had genuinely learned this material would produce a letter-count spread close to
which four numbers?

If a scoring procedure chose option C zero times out of twenty, what is the highest score it
could possibly reach on this bank?

The naive procedure scored 25.0% and the rotation procedure scored 15.0%. Which of the two is
closer to the truth about what this model knows, and why is that a trick question?

Solution

1. Close to the answer key: A two, B eight, C eight, D two. A model reading the options
should land on the right answer often, and the right answers are spread that way. A spread close
to five each would suggest a model guessing without a position preference, which is different
from a model that knows the material.

2. The correct answer is C on eight of the twenty questions, and a procedure that never
chooses C gets every one of those wrong. That leaves twelve questions it could possibly get
right, so the ceiling is 12 \div 20 = 0.60, which is 60%. The naive procedure has a
built-in maximum of 60% on this bank, and nothing the model knows can raise it. Worth sitting
with: a reported score has a ceiling set by the procedure, and the ceiling is almost never
mentioned.

3. It is a trick question because “closer to the truth” assumes there is a single true number
to be close to, and the consistency count of 1 out of 20 says there is not. The rotation
procedure is the better procedure, because it cannot be fooled by a position preference. But
its output of 15.0% is not a truer estimate of the model’s knowledge; it is a more honest
statement that there is nothing here to estimate. The right answer to “what does this model score”
is “under what procedure, and with what interval, and here is the consistency count.”

scored on the same twenty statistics questions. The only thing that differs between the bars is
the rule used to decide which option the model picked. The dashed line at 25% is the chance level
from Formula 13.2, and it is arithmetic rather than a measurement: with four options, guessing

records.content:
A reasonable reader reaches this point and draws the wrong conclusion. It goes like this:
“Position bias inflates naive scores. So every naive score is inflated by roughly ten points, and
I should mentally subtract ten from anything I read.”

That would be tidy. It is also wrong, and the evidence against it is in the course lab.

The same twenty questions were put to three models from the same family: the 0.5B, the 1.5B and
the 3B. Same questions, same prompts, same code, same machine. Size is the only thing that
changes, which makes this a controlled experiment in the ordinary scientific sense. Each model
was scored twice, once by the naive letter procedure and once by the rotation procedure. The
distance between those two scores is what this section calls the debiasing gap.

Here is what the gap did as the models got bigger.

At 0.5B, the gap is 10 points: 25.0% naive, 15.0% rotated.
At 1.5B, the gap is 10 points: 80.0% naive, 70.0% rotated.
At 3B, the gap is 0 points: 95.0% naive, 95.0% rotated.

The largest model’s score does not move when you take the position bias away. Rotating the
options changes nothing, because it was never answering on position in the first place.

And look at how the 3B distributed its first-pick answers: B eight times, C seven, D twice, A
three times. Now put the answer key beside it: B eight, C eight, D two, A two. Those two lines
are nearly the same line. The model is not picking positions. It is picking answers, and the
answers happen to sit where they sit.

The consistency counts tell the same story from the other side. Under four rotations, the number
of questions where all four rotations agreed on the verdict went 1, then 13, then 18, out of
twenty.

So position bias is not a tax levied on all benchmark scores. It is a symptom that appears when
a model does not know the answer. When a model has no view about which option is right, the only
thing left to break the tie is a habit, and a preference for the letter A is such a habit. When
the model does have a view, the habit is overridden and the bias vanishes on its own.

That reframes the diagnosis in section 13.3. The 16-out-of-20 A count was not a separate defect
sitting alongside a weak model. It was what a weak model looks like when you score it that
way.

Formula 13.8: The debiasing gap

1. In words. Score the model twice, once with the naive procedure and once with a procedure
that removes the position preference. Subtract the second score from the first. A large answer
means the naive score was propped up by something other than knowledge. An answer of zero means
the position preference was not doing any work.

2. The formula.\Delta = \hat{p}^{(\text{naive})} - \hat{p}^{(\text{rot})}

3. The symbols.

Symbol

How to say it out loud

What it means

\Delta

“delta”

a capital Greek D. In this book it marks a difference between two things. Here, the answer. See 

the toolkit on Greek letters

=

“equals”

the two sides are the same number

\hat{p}^{(\text{naive})}

“p hat under naive”

the accuracy under the naive letter procedure

\hat{p}^{(\text{rot})}

“p hat under rot”

the accuracy under the rotation procedure

the raised label in brackets

“under”

a label naming a procedure, never a power

-

“minus”

subtract the second from the first

4. Out loud. “The debiasing gap is the naive accuracy minus the rotation accuracy.”

5. Worked, on all three models.

The 0.5B model.\Delta = 0.25 - 0.15 = 0.10, \qquad 0.10 \times 100 = 10.0 \text{ percentage points}

The 1.5B model.\Delta = 0.80 - 0.70 = 0.10, \qquad 0.10 \times 100 = 10.0 \text{ percentage points}

The 3B model.\Delta = 0.95 - 0.95 = 0.00, \qquad 0.00 \times 100 = 0.0 \text{ percentage points}

6. Check it. \Delta can be negative, and that is informative rather than an error: it would
mean the debiased procedure scored higher, which happens when a model’s position habit was
pushing it away from correct answers rather than towards them.

The honest caution, and it belongs here rather than in a footnote. Each of these numbers comes
from twenty questions. A difference of one question is 5 percentage points on a bank this size.
The file lab/out/lab4_size_ladder.json carries a measured standard error for each rotation
score, and they are large: 0.0798 at 0.5B, 0.1025 at 1.5B and 0.0487 at 3B, which as percentage
points is 8.0, 10.2 and 4.9. Every score in this section should be read with a wobble of about
that size around it.
The 0-point gap at 3B is built on the model getting 19 of 20 both times. If the 3B had missed one
extra question under rotation, the gap would read 5 points instead of 0. So the shape of the
ladder, large gap at the bottom and no gap at the top, is the finding here. The precise gap
values are far less certain than printing them to one decimal place suggests, and


Chapter 12 is the chapter that taught you why.

Definition 13.8: Debiasing gap

The debiasing gap is the naive score minus the debiased score, in percentage points. A large
gap says the naive procedure was rewarding a position habit. A gap of zero says the model was
answering the question.

column does support is the qualitative claim: the gap is present when the model is weak and
absent when it is strong.

Try it 13.2: Reading the ladder

Using only the printed table:

The 1.5B model chose A four times out of twenty. Compute its over-choice ratio for A, using
Formula 13.4.

The 0.5B chose A sixteen times. Compute the same ratio, and say how many times larger it is.

Somebody claims “the 1.5B still has a position bias, because its naive and rotation scores
differ by 10 points.” Is the letter spread consistent with that claim?

Solution

1. The expected count is E = n/k = 20 \div 4 = 5. SoR_A = \frac{4}{5} = 4 \div 5 = 0.8

That is below 1, meaning the 1.5B chose A slightly less often than an unbiased procedure
would.

2. For the 0.5B,R_A = \frac{16}{5} = 16 \div 5 = 3.2

And 3.2 \div 0.8 = 4.0, so the smaller model’s over-choice of A is four times the larger
model’s.

3. The letter spread does not support a simple A-preference for the 1.5B. Its spread is
{'C': 7, 'B': 7, 'D': 2, 'A': 4}, which is close to the key on D and not wildly off on the
others, and it under-chooses A rather than over-choosing it. So whatever is costing the 1.5B
those 10 points under rotation is not a plain preference for the first option. It is more likely
that on the questions it does not know, its answer is unstable, and instability costs you under a
majority-of-four rule. You could check that directly by pulling out the per-question rotation
votes, which is Stretch problem 21 at the end of this chapter.

records.content:
Everything so far has been about one model. Almost every real question is about two.

Should the department install the 1.5B or the 3B? The 3B is more accurate and costs more energy
per token, a trade-off 

Chapter 7 measured. But before that trade-off is even worth
discussing, somebody has to establish that the 3B is actually better, and by how much, and with
what certainty.

The two models sat the same twenty questions, under the same rotation-debiased procedure.

Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct scored 14 of 20, which is 70.0%.

Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct scored 19 of 20, which is 95.0%.

The gap is 25.0 percentage points.

Now, how uncertain is that 25-point gap? There are two ways to work it out and they differ in
one assumption.

The unpaired way treats the two results as two separate surveys. You worked out the wobble
for one model’s score in 

Chapter 12; do that twice and combine. This is the standard
formula for comparing two proportions and it is in every introductory statistics book.

It is also the wrong tool here, and the reason is a single sentence: the two models answered
the same questions.

Think about what that means. Question 5 of the bank is hard, or it is easy, and it is exactly as
hard or as easy for both models. That shared difficulty is not noise to be averaged away. It is
information you paid for by using the same bank, and the unpaired formula throws it in the bin.

The paired way keeps it. Go through the questions one at a time and write down, for each one,
what the 3B did minus what the 1.5B did. That difference can only be three things: +1 if the 3B
got it right and the 1.5B did not, -1 if the reverse, and 0 if they did the same thing.

Then average those twenty differences. The average comes out to exactly the same 25 points, as it
always must. But the spread of the differences is smaller than the spread of the two separate
scores, because every question the models agreed on contributes a 0, and zeros pull a spread
down.

Smaller spread, smaller standard error, narrower interval. Same data, better answer, no extra
questions asked.
